# 1. Introduction

Modern vehicles are increasingly capable of perceiving their immediate environment with high fidelity. Radar, lidar, camera arrays, and ultrasonic sensors feed local perception stacks that maintain a rich model of the world inside a single vehicle. The limit of that model is the vehicle’s own sensor envelope: roughly 200 meters of useful range, heavily degraded by weather, occlusion, and geometry.

Cooperative perception breaks that limit. When vehicles share their local perception with each other and with roadside infrastructure, each participant gains a world model that extends far beyond its own sensors, sees around corners, and persists through weather and occlusion. The safety and efficiency gains are well-understood in the literature and are the subject of active standards work at SAE, ETSI, IEEE, and 3GPP.

The problem is not the absence of standards. The problem is that the existing standards ecosystem is fragmented across radio layers, message sets, security frameworks, and regional profiles, and leaves several practical questions unanswered. How do vehicles with different sensor suites produce interoperable perception output? How is trust established and revoked in real time without a continuously-available backhaul? How do driver-authorized cooperative behaviors (platoons, merges, intersection assist) form and dissolve safely?

O-CPS answers these questions by composing existing standards where they are adequate and specifying the missing pieces in a single coherent profile. It is deliberately thin. It adds the minimum necessary primitives on top of the existing V2X stack and refuses to invent new radio layers, new cryptographic primitives, or new market structures.

## 1.1 Design Heritage

O-CPS draws directly on three bodies of prior work. From SAE J2735 and J3161 it inherits the BSM/PSM message family and the PC5-based safety messaging conventions. From ETSI TS 103 324 it inherits the Collective Perception Message (CPM) concept and the perceived-object container model. From IEEE 1609.2 and ETSI TS 103 097 it inherits the pseudonym certificate and misbehavior-reporting frameworks. None of these are wholly sufficient in isolation; O-CPS is the profile that binds them together and fills the gaps.

## 1.2 Relationship to Strynex

“Strynex” is the reference implementation and vehicle-facing brand for an O-CPS stack. The two names are deliberately distinct: O-CPS is the open specification that any automaker, supplier, or municipality may implement without royalty; Strynex is one concrete implementation and a set of optional application-layer overlays (notably Slipstream Mode, §13) that sit on top of the base profile. A vehicle may advertise O-CPS conformance without implementing any Strynex-branded overlay, and the protocol MUST continue to interoperate correctly.
